title: Dairying and lactase persistence
summary: Fat residues in ancient pots show people milking domestic animals in north-west Anatolia by the seventh millennium BCE, and milk use was widespread in Europe from the Neolithic on. Early farmers mostly could not digest milk sugar as adults. Lactase persistence, the ability to do so, became the most strongly selected single-gene trait of the last 10,000 years in Europe and parts of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia. Its main European variant began to be favoured about 7,500 years ago between the central Balkans and central Europe.

uncertainty.note: Earliest milk residues in the 7th millennium BCE (Evershed et al. 2022); selection for the -13,910*T allele from about 7,500 years ago (Itan et al. 2009). Both continue later.

as_recorded.calendar: BCE, organic residue analysis of pottery fats
as_recorded.value: earliest organic residue-based evidence of dairying locates to 7 th millennium BCE northwest Anatolia

as_recorded.calendar: Years ago, Bayesian inference on ancient DNA and allele frequencies
as_recorded.value: −13,910*T allele first underwent selection among dairying farmers around 7,500 years ago

where.modern_name: Northwestern Anatolia (stand-in pin at Barcın Höyük, Bursa Province, Turkey; early dairying spread across Europe)
where.historical_name: Northwestern Anatolia during the Early Neolithic (no recorded polities)

importance.justification: Made milk a lifelong food for many peoples, the strongest recent genetic adaptation in humans (R3 D3 T4 L2).

related.because: The domestication of ruminants provided the milk supply that initiated dairy technology and subsequent selection for lactase persistence.

beats.caption: Neolithic farming communities in northwestern Anatolia began processing ruminant milk in ceramic vessels.
Strong natural selection favoured the lactase persistence allele, allowing adult milk digestion across European populations.
